summary: Defines a way to attach extra data to OSPF packets so routers on a link can exchange arbitrary information not fitting the standard formats. This RFC is experimental, and it was replaced by RFC 5613.

eli5.summary: The standard OSPF message form has no spare room. This adds a flexible attachment for extra notes between neighbors. It was later replaced.

questions: how do ospf routers exchange extra capabilities
subtitle: Attach extra data to OSPF packets for link-local exchange of capabilities.

tldr.problem: Standard OSPF packet formats have limited room for routers to exchange information about capabilities or operational state. The existing Options field in OSPF messages has few available bits left.
tldr.mechanism: LLS adds an optional data block at the end of OSPF Hello and Database Description packets. This block contains type-length-value (TLV) fields that vendors and extensions can populate with arbitrary data without breaking standard OSPF.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now exchange vendor-specific information and signal capabilities on a link. The extension is backward-compatible because non-LLS routers simply ignore the extra data.

today: RFC 4813 is Experimental and has been superseded by RFC 5613, which modernizes the link-local signaling mechanism.

sections.title: The Problem of Inflexible OSPF Packet Formats
sections.content:
OSPF is a link-state routing protocol where routers exchange information to build a consistent map of the network. The OSPF packet format is well-defined and rigid. Hello packets and Database Description (DBD) packets include an Options field, but this field has limited space and most bits are already assigned for standard OSPF features.

As OSPF evolves, implementers and vendors sometimes need to exchange additional information on a link without creating new OSPF packet types or modifying core message structures. RFC 4813 solves this by introducing a Link-Local Signaling (LLS) extension that adds an optional data block at the end of existing OSPF packets.
sections.eli5: OSPF messages follow a strict format with no room for notes. This RFC lets you add a note at the end that new routers read and old ones ignore.

sections.title: LLS Data Block Structure and Format
sections.content:
The LLS data block is appended after the standard OSPF message and any authentication data, but is included in the IP packet length. The block begins with a checksum field and an LLS Data Length field (in 32-bit words), followed by a series of TLV triplets.

Each TLV contains a Type field identifying the data kind, a Length field for the value size in bytes, and a variable-length Value field containing the actual data. All TLVs are padded to 32-bit boundaries, though padding bytes are not counted in the TLV length field. This structure allows vendors to define custom TLVs for their own purposes.
sections.eli5: The data block starts with a checksum and length, then has labeled sections (TLVs) where each section says what it is and how long it is.

sections.title: The L-bit and Predefined TLVs
sections.content:
To signal that an OSPF message carries LLS data, a new L-bit is defined in the Options field with value 0x10. Routers set this bit in Hello and DBD packets when they include the LLS data block. Routers that do not support LLS simply ignore the bit and the extra data.

The RFC defines two standard TLV types: the Extended Options (EO) TLV for announcing link-specific capabilities using a 32-bit flags field, and the Cryptographic Authentication (CA) TLV for signing the LLS block when OSPF cryptographic authentication is enabled. The CA-TLV includes a sequence number matching the OSPF packet's sequence number to prevent replay attacks.
sections.eli5: The L-bit is a flag saying "I have extra data attached." Standard TLVs exist for extra options and for cryptographic signatures.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Extensibility
sections.content:
LLS is completely backward-compatible. Routers that support LLS set the L-bit and routers that do not support it simply ignore the flag and the extra data block. There is no requirement for all routers in a network to support LLS; they can coexist peacefully on the same link.

The RFC reserves LLS type values 0-32767 for IETF-consensus allocation and values 32768-65535 for private and experimental use. This allows vendors to define proprietary TLVs and experimenters to test new LLS extensions without worrying about collisions. Future OSPF extensions can allocate their own TLV types as needed.
sections.eli5: Old routers ignore the extra data. New routers can add their own TLVs in a reserved space. Everyone gets along.
